claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: OnTrack monitors agent trajectories in real-time, taking about a millisecond per step.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: To overcome this issue, we propose OnTrack, a streaming monitoring mechanism that, as the agent progresses in its task, compares its steps and the dependencies between them against recorded successful runs and alerts the user of potential issues or blocks the agent, taking about a millisecond per step.

evidence_spans.source_text: Measured on an Apple M5 Max core, the fast path runs at p50 0.85 ms / p95 1.6 ms per event at t=m=40, K=3 (p50 0.5 / p95 0.7 ms at t=m=20; p50 1.6 / p95 3.9 ms at t=80)
per-event runtime spans 0.2–1.6 ms.

evidence_spans.source_text: OnTrack provides early-trajectory discrimination that outperforms cosine similarity where it matters most — the first ten steps (+0.057 AUROC at k=8 under the primary held-out protocol, instance-level bootstrap 95% CI [+0.033, +0.080], excluding zero through k=10)

claims.label: partially_supported
claims.claim_summary: An abort policy saves ~18% compute with 83% precision on failing runs.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: Additionally, by deploying an abort policy on top of it, we save ∼18% of the compute that would have been burned on agents heading to failure, and 83% of runs that were interrupted were actually heading to failure (5 out of every 6 aborts were correct).

evidence_spans.source_text: At threshold 0.60 (Table 6), 23.3% of unresolved traces are stopped early at a 20.7% false-stop rate, yielding 17.9% cost savings on the unresolved population.

Because the corpus base rate is heavily skewed toward failure (81% unresolved), the balanced-sample false-stop rates translate to ≈83% precision in deployment: five of six aborted runs would indeed have failed.

One protocol disclosure: the full threshold sweep is reported, and 0.60 is an illustrative threshold selected for exposition after the sweep — not a recommended deployment setting, since it was not chosen on held-out data.

evidence_spans.source_text: The active set and its lookahead are At = { j : every reference-parent of j is satisfied }, Lt = children(At) \ At, with roots vacuously active, and the masked marginal is ν(t) j = νj (j ∈At ∪{satisfied}), βlook νj (j ∈Lt), εν νj otherwise

Proposition 2 (Relabeling invariance of the masked objective). Fix a covered sub-DAG, a mask ν(t), and structural weights that are order-independent (age weights matched across comparisons or disabled). Then the masked objective, and its exact minimizer set from a permutation-equivariant initialization, are invariant to graph-preserving relabelings of the prefix: the satisfied set, active set A, and masked marginal ν(t) are functions of the covered sub-DAG alone, and members of an executable antichain carry full mass simultaneously, so no order among them is preferred.
Scenario B finalizes to the in-order score exactly (0.913 = 0.913), the empirical face of Prop. 2.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Amortized warm-started iterations keep per-step execution time down to about one millisecond.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: For S3, instead of re-solving the alignment at every step, we take one warm-started iteration of the batch solver per event — about a millisecond per step — and run the solver to convergence only before acting on an intervention (Sec. 4.3).

evidence_spans.source_text: Two-tier escalation. The fast path above runs on every event. If and only if it raises a would-be intervention verdict, the evaluator escalates to a converged solve (≤10 outer CG, ≤50 inner Sinkhorn, cold tolerance) on the current prefix before the verdict is confirmed.

Measured on an Apple M5 Max core, the fast path runs at p50 0.85 ms / p95 1.6 ms per event at t=m=40, K=3 (p50 0.5 / p95 0.7 ms at t=m=20; p50 1.6 / p95 3.9 ms at t=80); the escalated solve matches the batch-solve runtime (≈30 ms) and is invoked only ahead of interventions.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: OnTrack's final solve aligns with batch evaluation when online dependency extraction matches.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: At the end of the run, one final solve makes the monitor’s output identical to the batch evaluator’s — provided the dependencies discovered online match what batch extraction would find (Prop. 1).

evidence_spans.source_text: Let the stream terminate at t = n, let the online dependency graph equal the graph a batch evaluator would extract from the completed log, and let OnTrack perform one cold-started converged solve with the frontier mask removed and marginals renormalized to the batch convention. Then the finalization computation — the same deterministic implemented procedure (clipped GW linearization and surrogate diagnostic, Sec. 4.3; we say procedure rather than objective because a clipped gradient need not be the gradient of any objective), constraint set, parameters (θ, λ, ε), references, node costs, initialization, and stopping schedule, with age weights disabled (batch convention) — is identical to a batch evaluator running the same released implementation on the completed trajectory, and the deterministic solver returns the same score.

Proof sketch. With the mask removed and marginals renormalized, every input to the solver coincides with the batch invocation, and a deterministic solver run from the same canonical initialization produces the same iterates.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: OnTrack and baselines show comparable, modest trajectory-level outcome separation.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: On a balanced sample (50 resolved, 50 unresolved), no method reliably separates outcomes (Table 8): OnTrack reaches 0.581, cosine 0.643, with widely overlapping bootstrap CIs.

evidence_spans.source_text: Bootstrap 95% CI: OnTrack score [0.466, 0.689], cosine [0.531, 0.759] — overlapping.

Point estimates are unstable at this sample size — an independent draw of the evaluation sample yields OnTrack 0.666 vs. cosine 0.657, reversing the ordering — so the only conclusion the data support is that neither process alignment nor content similarity predicts patch correctness from the trajectory alone.

claims.label: supported
claims.claim_summary: Trajectory outcome prediction collapses near chance when step length is controlled.
claims.claim_text_verbatim: When resolved/unresolved pairs are matched within ±3 steps (50 pairs, mean 30.6 steps in both classes), all trajectory-level signals collapse toward chance: OnTrack score 0.526, cosine 0.540, n steps 0.500 by construction.

evidence_spans.source_text: When resolved/unresolved pairs are matched within ±3 steps (50 pairs, mean 30.6 steps in both classes), all trajectory-level signals collapse toward chance: OnTrack score 0.526, cosine 0.540, n steps 0.500 by construction.

This confirms that the modest full-trajectory outcome correlation is largely mediated by trace length — unresolved traces are longer on average — and that OnTrack score is length-sensitive by construction (more steps → more accumulated transport cost).
